meta.audience: Benjamin's sons, then all the people of Zarahemla

world_behind.title: A succession scene in the Israelite shape
world_behind.text: Benjamin says he must "go the way of all the earth," which is the formula David uses to Solomon and Joshua uses at his farewell (Josh. 23:14). What follows is what follows there: instruction to the heir, a charge concerning the kingdom, and an assembly. The record is running a known pattern.

world_behind.title: Royal regalia, itemized
world_behind.text: Verse 16 transfers four objects, and ancient kingship was conveyed by objects as much as by words. What is striking is the set: a library, a weapon, and a navigational instrument. Nothing resembling a crown, a throne, or an anointing oil appears anywhere in the transfer.

world_behind.title: The director, before it has a name
world_behind.text: The instrument that led Lehi through the wilderness is called "the ball or director" here. It receives the name Liahona only much later, in Alma. At this point in the record it is a functional description of a working object being handed to a king.

world_behind.title: Egyptian literacy, supplied as the mechanism
world_behind.text: Verse 4 explains why Lehi could read the brass plates: he had been taught in the language of the Egyptians. The reader was told at the very beginning that Nephi's learning included it. Four hundred and seventy years later a king uses that fact to make an argument about why his sons can read at all.

world_behind.title: A name conferred at a coronation
world_behind.text: Benjamin announces he will give the people a name to distinguish them, and that it can be lost only through transgression. Ancient enthronement ceremonies regularly involved naming, and the name itself is withheld until Mosiah 5, four chapters later.

world_behind.title: The argument from what would have been lost
world_behind.text: Verses 3 through 5 argue that without the plates they would have suffered in ignorance and their fathers would have dwindled in unbelief. Amaleki had made the same argument about the people of Zarahemla two pages earlier, from observation. Benjamin makes it as a hypothetical, about himself.

words.text: Things known only by disclosure. Benjamin says the plates are why they are not ignorant of them, which locates the mysteries in a readable text. Whatever is hidden here is hidden in a book that a literate person can open.

To bestow formally. Benjamin thought it expedient to confer the kingdom on one of his sons. It is the same verb Omni used of handing on the plates. Kingship and custody of the record are transferred with one word in this book, and in verse 16 they are transferred in one act.

A public announcement with legal force. Mosiah is made to issue one before he is made king, so his first royal act precedes his kingship. The chapter's mechanism for gathering a nation is a document read aloud, which is what the whole book is about to depend on.

The prophets use adultery for covenant unfaithfulness, not only for the marriage offense: Israel is the wife who goes after other gods. Benjamin warns that this people could "become a wicked and an adulterous people" (v. 13), the pairing Matthew gives to Jesus (Matt. 16:4) about the generation that keeps asking for a sign. Five centuries lie between them, and in both the charge is that people already bound to God went looking elsewhere. The word is used once in this record.

cites.quote: become a wicked and an adulterous people

spans.text: become a wicked and an adulterous people

words.text: In older English a victim was the creature brought to the altar. By the period of this translation the word had moved to mean a person destroyed by someone else's will, and that is the sense here: without God's arm the fathers would have "become victims to their hatred" (v. 14). Benjamin has just said that preservation can stop. This is what he says lies on the other side of its stopping, and he puts it as something people would do to them rather than as a judgment. The King James Bible never uses the word.

Forward movement, used here of a journey that stalls. The unfaithful "did not prosper nor progress," and the two verbs are paired. Prospering is the covenant word; progressing is the physical one. Benjamin puts them together and treats one as the visible form of the other.

phrases.term: Taught in all the language of his fathers, that thereby they might become men of understanding
phrases.text: Language first, understanding second, in that causal order. The princes' education is described as linguistic before it is moral or military, and the stated purpose is comprehension of prophecy. It is the clearest picture in the record of what a royal education was for.

phrases.term: Were it not for these plates... we must have suffered in ignorance
phrases.text: An argument by absence. Benjamin is not praising the record; he is describing the state he would be in without it, and the state he names is ignorance. The case for scripture here is made on the grounds of information.

phrases.term: He having been taught in the language of the Egyptians therefore he could read these engravings
phrases.text: A chain of causes reaching back four and a half centuries: Lehi's schooling made the plates readable, which made teaching possible, which made transmission possible, which is why Benjamin's sons know anything. The verse is an argument about literacy dressed as family history.

phrases.term: Our fathers would have dwindled in unbelief
phrases.text: The verb that describes the Lamanites' condition from the first book onward, applied here to his own line as a possibility narrowly avoided. Benjamin's claim is that his people had a book. The difference is circumstantial and he says so.

phrases.term: The traditions of their fathers, which are not correct
phrases.text: The record's flattest statement of what went wrong with the Lamanites, and it is about information. Inherited error, transmitted faithfully. It is the same diagnosis Jacob offered when he traced their hostility to their fathers, and it leaves room for the remedy Enos prayed for.

phrases.term: We can know of their surety because we have them before our eyes
phrases.text: An argument from possession. The plates are true and the proof offered is that they can be inspected. It is an unusually physical warrant for a claim about scripture, and it is offered to sons who are holding the objects.

phrases.term: Search them diligently, that ye may profit thereby
phrases.text: Two imperatives, and the second is about return on effort. Benjamin does not tell his sons to revere the records or to preserve them; he tells them to search and to profit. Custody has already been dealt with in verse 16; this is about use.

phrases.term: A name that never shall be blotted out, except it be through transgression
phrases.text: A gift with one condition and no expiry. Blotting out is the language of erasure from a register, which suits a name given at an assembly and recorded. Benjamin announces the terms four chapters before he announces the name.

phrases.term: He will no more preserve them by his matchless and marvelous power
phrases.text: The preservation is presented as ongoing and as revocable. Benjamin's warning is that God will stop doing what he has been doing, and the result named is weakness. The word "hitherto" in the same verse carries the argument.

phrases.term: The sword of Laban, and the ball or director, which led our fathers through the wilderness
phrases.text: Two objects from the founding generation, handed over together. One was taken in a street in Jerusalem and one appeared outside a tent door. Between them they represent the two ways the record says this people survived: force and guidance. A king now holds both.

phrases.term: According to the heed and diligence which they gave unto him
phrases.text: The operating principle of the director, stated as a rule instead of as a story. Attention and effort are the inputs; direction is the output. Benjamin gives his son the instrument and the manual in the same sentence.

phrases.term: They were smitten with famine and sore afflictions, to stir them up in remembrance of their duty
phrases.text: Affliction assigned a purpose, and the purpose is memory. This is the same clause Lehi was given about the Lamanites as a scourge, turned now on the covenant people themselves and applied to a wilderness journey the audience knows the outcome of.

verses.label: v. 2
verses.title: Education described as access to a text
verses.text: The record states what the sons were taught and why in a single clause: "he caused that they should be taught in all the language of his fathers, that thereby they might become men of understanding; and that they might know concerning the prophecies which had been spoken by the mouths of their fathers." Understanding is presented as a consequence of language, and language as the means to a body of writing. Nothing about virtue, warfare, or government appears in the curriculum.

verses.label: v. 8
verses.title: An omission conceded at once
verses.text: Immediately after the instruction ends the record marks what it has not printed: "many more things did king Benjamin teach his sons, which are not written in this book." The phrase in this book is doing precise work, since the volume elsewhere distinguishes between what is unwritten and what is written on other plates. Here the material is simply absent, and no reason is given for the selection.

verses.label: v. 11–12
verses.title: A promise with its exception written into it
verses.text: The record announces the name with a guarantee and a condition in adjacent clauses: "I give unto them a name that never shall be blotted out, except it be through transgression." Verse 13 then works out what happens if the exception applies, "if this highly favored people of the Lord should fall into transgression... the Lord will deliver up their strength." A record that is about to spend a chapter on the giving of the name states the terms of its loss first.

verses.label: v. 15–16
verses.title: Four objects handed over, and they are listed
verses.text: The record reports the transfer of power in two parts, and makes the second an inventory: "he gave him charge concerning all the affairs of the kingdom. And moreover, he also gave him charge concerning the records which were engraven on the plates of brass; and also the plates of Nephi; and also the sword of Laban, and the ball or director." Two sets of plates, a weapon, and an instrument. The kingdom takes one clause; the objects take four.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: A mechanism explained as conditional
verses.text: The record supplies an operating rule for one of the objects rather than a description of it: "as they were unfaithful they did not prosper nor progress in their journey, but were driven back, and incurred the displeasure of God upon them; and therefore they were smitten with famine and sore afflictions, to stir them up in remembrance of their duty." The same behaviour is reported at 1 Ne. 16:28–29, where the pointers work "according to the faith and diligence and heed" given them. An instrument is described by the condition under which it stops working.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: The chapter ends by setting up the next one
verses.text: The last verse is administrative: Mosiah "proclaimed unto all the people who were in the land of Zarahemla that thereby they might gather themselves together, to go up to the temple to hear the words which his father should speak unto them." Nothing is said or done. What the verse supplies is the mechanism by which the crowd of Mosiah 2 assembles, which is a proclamation, and the record puts it at the close of one chapter rather than the head of the next.

chapter.title: The case for scripture is made on informational grounds
chapter.text: Benjamin's argument is that without the plates they would not know things: the mysteries, the commandments, the prophecies. Not that they would be worse people first, but that they would be ignorant people, and worse follows from that. Verses 3 through 5 run the whole case that way.

chapter.title: The Lamanite difference is located in traditions, not in nature
chapter.text: Verse 5 says they know nothing of these things, or disbelieve them, because of traditions that are not correct. Benjamin's own people are one lost book away from the same position, and he says so about his own fathers. It is the least tribal explanation the record has offered.

chapter.title: Kingship is transferred as custody
chapter.text: Verses 15 and 16 use one verb for both transfers: "he gave him charge concerning all the affairs of the kingdom," and "he also gave him charge concerning the records which were engraven on the plates of brass; and also the plates of Nephi; and also, the sword of Laban, and the ball or director." Four objects in the second list and one office covering both. Mosiah 28:20 records the archive being handed to Alma rather than to a successor king, which is how the two functions are separated when the monarchy ends at Mosiah 29.

chapter.title: The regalia is a library, a weapon, and a compass
chapter.text: No crown, no throne, no oil. What a Nephite king receives is the means of knowing, the means of defending, and the means of being led. The third comes with a rule about why it stops working.

chapter.title: The name is announced before it is given
chapter.text: Four chapters separate the promise in verse 12 from the naming in Mosiah 5. The terms are published first: it distinguishes, it was earned by diligence, and only transgression can erase it. The delay makes the whole address a preparation for a single word.

chapter.title: Favor is described as maintenance
chapter.text: Verse 13 says God will "no more preserve them" if they transgress, and verse 14 says the fathers would have fallen without his arm. Preservation is continuous, active, and withdrawable. The chapter treats being a chosen people as a process.

chapter.title: The chapter is an overture
chapter.text: Peace, education, the value of records, a succession, a promised name, a warning, the regalia, and a gathering. Every one of these returns in the five chapters that follow. An opening chapter is meant to do that, and this one does.

applications.title: Teach the language first
applications.text: Benjamin's sons were taught the language of their fathers first, so that they could reach the prophecies themselves. Whatever you want someone to understand, give them the access rather than the summary.

applications.title: Ask what you would not know
applications.text: Take a particular book, teacher, or record and work out what you would be ignorant of without it. Benjamin's whole argument for scripture is built on that question.

applications.title: Check the traditions you inherited
applications.text: The chapter's diagnosis of an entire people is inherited error, faithfully transmitted. Identify one thing you believe mainly because you were raised in it, and test it.

applications.title: Search for profit
applications.text: The instruction is to search diligently in order to gain something. Read the next thing you read with a specific question you actually want answered.

applications.title: Give heed and diligence
applications.text: The director worked in proportion to attention and effort, and stopped when they lapsed. When guidance seems absent, the chapter's first diagnostic is your own heed.

applications.title: Treat favor as maintenance
applications.text: Nothing you have been given is a permanent status. Name one blessing you have been treating as settled, and ask what keeping it actually requires of you.

questions.text: What would I not know if I had never had the books I have?
Which of my beliefs are traditions I have never examined?
Do I treat scripture as something I can check, or only as something I am told?
When did I last search something diligently rather than read it dutifully?
Where am I assuming God's help will continue regardless of what I do?
In what part of my life have I stopped giving heed, and what has stopped moving as a result?
